This is a box plot comparing inference latency across four different hardware platforms.

The horizontal axis is labeled Hardware and contains four categories: CPU, GPU, TPU, and Edge NPU. The vertical axis is labeled Latency in milliseconds, running linearly from zero to nearly two hundred milliseconds with tick marks every twenty-five milliseconds.

There is no legend as all boxes use the same solid blue color.

For CPU, the median latency is about 116 milliseconds, with an interquartile range between approximately 106 and 142 milliseconds, spanning from a minimum of about 68 to a maximum of 190 milliseconds. For GPU, the median is roughly 17 milliseconds, with the middle fifty percent falling between 14 and 20 milliseconds, and a single outlier near 29 milliseconds. For TPU, the median latency is the lowest at about 11 milliseconds, an interquartile range from 9 to 14 milliseconds, and a few outliers between 22 and 24 milliseconds. For Edge NPU, the median is about 44 milliseconds, with an interquartile range between 37 and 48 milliseconds, whiskers extending from 24 to 62 milliseconds, and multiple high outliers reaching up to about 87 milliseconds.

Overall, latency is ranked from fastest to slowest as TPU, followed closely by GPU, then Edge NPU, with CPU being by far the slowest and exhibiting the largest variance. Edge NPU displays a noticeable tail of several high-latency outliers.

This is a split violin plot titled Effect of chain-of-thought prompting, comparing performance score distributions with and without chain-of-thought across three tasks. 

The horizontal axis shows three tasks: Math, Code, and Writing. The vertical axis shows the score on a linear scale starting at 20 and extending to 110. 

A legend in the upper right defines two conditions: Without CoT represented in blue on the left side of each violin, and With CoT represented in orange on the right side. Internal horizontal dashed lines indicate the median, while dotted lines show the upper and lower quartiles.

For Math, Without CoT has a median score of approximately 56 with quartiles at about 48 and 62, whereas With CoT shows a substantial increase, reaching a median of about 74 with quartiles at roughly 67 and 79 and maximum values exceeding 100. 

For Code, Without CoT has a median of about 55 with quartiles near 49 and 62, while With CoT shifts upward to a median of about 64 and quartiles at 58 and 70, with upper tails extending near 97. 

For Writing, the distributions are very similar: Without CoT has a median of roughly 54, and With CoT has a median of roughly 56, both spanning between approximately 25 and 85 with interquartile ranges around 48 to 64.

Overall, chain-of-thought prompting provides the largest benefit on Math, a moderate improvement on Code, and almost no change on Writing.

This is a scatter plot with a fitted linear regression line showing the relationship between compute and throughput, titled Compute versus throughput, r equals 0.94.

The horizontal axis represents GPU hours in thousands, plotted on a linear scale ranging from 0 to roughly 10. The vertical axis represents throughput in tokens per second in thousands, plotted on a linear scale with tick marks from 5 to 25, extending down near 1.

There is a single data series shown as semi-transparent blue dots, accompanied by a solid blue regression line with a narrow shaded confidence band.

In terms of key numbers, at close to 0 thousand GPU hours, the regression line starts at about 5.5 thousand tokens per second. The lowest data points drop to around 2.5 thousand tokens per second near 0.6 thousand GPU hours. At the upper end, near 10 thousand GPU hours, the regression line reaches roughly 25 thousand tokens per second, with the highest data point reaching about 26 thousand tokens per second near 8.6 thousand GPU hours.

The main pattern is a strong, steady positive linear correlation, confirmed by the correlation coefficient of 0.94. Throughput increases proportionally with GPU hours, with data points remaining evenly distributed along the regression line across the entire measured range without extreme outliers.

This line chart shows the scaling of test error with increasing dataset size for three different optimizers.

The horizontal axis represents dataset size in tokens on a logarithmic scale, ranging from 10 to the 6th power to 10 to the 10th power. The vertical axis represents error on a linear scale from below 1.0 up to just over 3.0, with gridlines spaced every 0.5 units; it does not start at zero. Shaded bands around each line indicate uncertainty or variance.

The legend lists three optimizers: SGD in blue, Adam in orange, and Muon in green.

All three lines start at nearly the same point at 10 to the 6th tokens, with an error of about 2.98. As data size increases to 10 to the 10th tokens, the error decreases steadily for all methods. At the final point of 10 to the 10th tokens, SGD reaches an error of approximately 1.34, Adam reaches about 1.15, and Muon reaches about 0.91.

Overall, test error decreases monotonically for all three optimizers as dataset size grows. Muon consistently achieves the lowest error at every point beyond 10 to the 6th tokens, Adam ranks second, and SGD performs the worst. The performance gap between the optimizers widens as the dataset size increases.

This figure consists of two side-by-side line charts displaying training progress and hyperparameter tuning results. 

The left panel, labeled a, shows accuracy on the vertical axis from about zero point two to one point zero versus training epoch on the horizontal axis from zero to thirty. The right panel, labeled b, shows final validation accuracy from zero point six to zero point nine on the vertical axis against learning rate on a logarithmic horizontal axis spanning from ten to the power of minus four to ten to the power of minus two. Neither vertical axis starts at zero.

Panel a contains two curves: a blue line for training accuracy and an orange line for validation accuracy, along with a vertical dashed gray line at epoch twelve. Both curves start at approximately zero point two six at epoch one and rise together to around zero point nine two at epoch twelve. After this point, the training accuracy continues to rise smoothly, approaching one point zero at epoch thirty, while the validation accuracy peaks near zero point nine five around epoch seventeen before declining to about zero point eight seven at epoch thirty.

Panel b plots a single blue line with five square data points. Validation accuracy starts at about zero point eight one at a learning rate of ten to the power of minus four, rises through zero point eight six to a maximum of approximately zero point eight nine at ten to the power of minus three, drops to zero point eight four, and falls steeply to about zero point six two at ten to the power of minus two.
